quick_take.text: A huge red horse charges through the middle while workers strain to hold it back. Behind them you can see scaffolding and factory chimneys: a new part of Milan going up. The horse is the raw energy of the growing city, all muscle and motion. The canvas is big, about 2 by 3 metres, and it's often called Boccioni's first major Futurist painting.

quick_take.text: A crowd rushes toward a fight outside a café in Milan's Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, a glass-roofed shopping arcade. Two women in the middle are going at it, and everyone else gets pulled in. The bright electric light is almost as much the subject as the people. Boccioni still uses small strokes of pure colour here, a technique called Divisionism that he used before Futurism.

quick_take.text: This is a goodbye at a train station, painted as a feeling instead of a snapshot. A steam locomotive sits in the middle, and wavy lines pull people into hugs. It's part of a series called 'States of Mind' about leaving and staying behind. The version you usually see today was repainted after Boccioni saw Cubism in Paris in 1911, which is why the shapes look broken up.

quick_take.text: It's a person on a bike, but don't look for a clear wheel or face. Boccioni broke the rider into overlapping shapes and lines to show speed, not looks. The idea is that something moving fast blends into the space around it. You're looking at movement itself, turned into a picture.

quick_take.text: A red car speeds through the picture, and the space around it splits into sharp, repeating arrow shapes. Those angles are the car's speed and roar pushing through the air. Russolo was a painter and also a musician. Around the same time, he wrote a manifesto about noise and built machines to make it.
